title: When MLLMs Miss What Humans Read: Diagnosing and Learning to Read Squint Text

paper.title: When MLLMs Miss What Humans Read: Diagnosing and Learning to Read Squint Text
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image’s coarse
structure—text a human recovers by squinting—and report that no text is
present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency,
motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench , comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl , a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight
analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is
weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the
correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as a major
bottleneck. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed
visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD : a frozen teacher receives a
downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and
its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories.
At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches
88.61 ANLS on SquintBench , versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone,
24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and
68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These
results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its
generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal LLMs can miss text embedded in an image’s coarse structure even when a human can recover it by squinting or viewing the image at reduced scale. We call this failure Squint Text ; we study why the visual evidence is difficult for current models to access and show that the corrective viewing condition can be internalized through training, enabling original-only inference. Modern VLMs are strong scene-text readers, yet this capability breaks sharply on Squint Text . As Figure 1 shows, frontier commercial and open-source models ( Singh et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) can report that no text is present even when the hidden string is readily recoverable by a person. The failure also persists with model scale (Table 3 ). Downscaling or low-pass filtering recovers part of the missing text, but leaves a substantial residual. Squint Text therefore exposes a specific recognition deficiency that stronger generic perception and inference-time preprocessing do not reliably remove. This deficiency matters in deployment. Images are widely used to carry illicit promotion and other policy-violating content ( Meta, 2026c ; Meta, 2026b ; X Corp., 2026 ; TikTok, 2026 ) , and the harmful semantics can reside in text drawn into the image rather than in the depicted scene ( Guo et al., 2024a ; Kiela et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) . In production moderation traffic, we observe domains, contact strings, and slogans embedded into coarse image structure so that human viewers can read them while the reviewing model reports no text. Such examples create a direct blind spot at the visual-review stage of an automated moderation pipeline ( Meta, 2026a ) . To study the failure, we introduce SquintBench , containing 1076 production moderation images, and SquintCtrl , a controlled synthetic suite for isolating what the model represents and where the failure arises. Frozen-weight diagnostics show that hidden text leaves a strong coarse signal, while glyph identity is only weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied. Controlled image interventions on SquintBench itself further show that suppressing high-frequency content can substantially improve reading at matched visual-token budgets, implicating high-frequency interference as a major contributor while leaving room for a secondary token-count effect. These findings motivate Squint OPSD : during training, a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distribution supervises a student that sees only the original image. At inference, the student receives the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench , compared with 26.50 for the base model and 58.96 when the corrective view is supplied only at inference. The capability transfers to external hidden-text benchmarks while retaining substantial general vision-language capability with measurable, task-dependent trade-offs. Analysis after training shows that glyph representations become more discriminative, reading depends causally on glyph-bearing regions under our visual-token embedding intervention, and the residual candidate distribution becomes more visually structured. Code and the evaluation suite are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Squint_Text-3456 .

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • A deployment-grounded failure mode and two complementary datasets. We define Squint Text and introduce SquintBench , comprising 1076 production moderation images, for realistic evaluation, together with SquintCtrl for controlled diagnosis of hidden-text representation, localization, and recoverability. • A diagnosis of why current MLLMs miss Squint Text . Hidden text leaves a strong coarse signal but weak glyph identity; the identity signal becomes more accessible at glyph-bearing locations, and high-frequency interference is a major contributor, with token count a possible secondary factor. • A diagnosis-driven training method. Squint OPSD uses a downscaled privileged view together with a ground-truth hint to provide token-level distributional supervision for original-only inference, reaching 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench . Figure 1: Squint Text , and why the deployed defence does not remove it. (a) Pipeline images whose embedded string a human reads—directly or by stepping back—while GPT, Gemini and Claude each answer “No text in this image” , on the original and the scaled view alike. (b) Downscaling before review recovers only part of the hidden text for every off-the-shelf model.

sections.heading: 2.1 Problem setting
sections.text: Given an image x x and an instruction to transcribe its text, the model must report every string a human reader would, including text carried in the image’s coarse structure. We use read-out to refer to the mapping from encoded visual representations to the generated transcription. Let v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) denote a bicubically downscaled view of x x , at 1 / 8 1/8 linear scale unless stated otherwise. We compare a single-image input x x with a two-view input ⟨ x , v ⟩ \langle x,v\rangle to test whether changing the viewing condition makes the same underlying visual evidence easier for a frozen model to use. Section 3 performs this comparison with identical off-the-shelf weights; the training method is introduced separately in Section 4 . On SquintBench we report ANLS ( Biten et al., 2019 ) , with predicted and reference regions matched as a set before scoring so that a correct transcription written in a different order is not penalised.

sections.heading: 2.2 Datasets
sections.text: Showing that the phenomenon occurs in deployment requires real model failures; attributing the failure to a particular mechanism requires controlled examples. We therefore use two complementary datasets. SquintBench comprises 1076 squint-text images collected from a production moderation pipeline. All 1076 examples are production-derived. These images are typically profile photos, in which a human reader recognizes the embedded text almost effortlessly. Human annotators transcribe all visible and hidden text. Thus, SquintBench is used as the realistic end-to-end evaluation set. SquintCtrl supplies the controlled counterpart. A glyph string is rendered as a binary conditioning image and embedded into a scene using QR Code Monster v2 ( Monster Labs, 2023 ) , a ControlNet ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) over Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , with scene prompts sampled from JourneyDB ( Sun et al., 2023 ) . For each controlled comparison, non-target generation variables are held fixed; because the conditioning image is known, each sample also has an exact token-level glyph mask without detector or human annotation. The four subsets serve distinct diagnostics. SquintCtrl-Pair contains 500 matched text-present/text-free pairs for testing whether hidden-text presence is encoded. The text-free member is regenerated through the same ControlNet branch using an all-black conditioning image, avoiding a synthesis pipeline shortcut. SquintCtrl-Glyph contains two 500-image closed vocabularies over ten Chinese glyphs ( 加女可度搜月百看网馊) and ten Latin letters for glyph-identity and localization analyses. SquintCtrl-Strength varies 200 scenes across 5 conditioning strengths to study the recoverability boundary. SquintCtrl-Read contains 200 open-vocabulary images for end-to-end read-out and post-training analysis. Detailed generation and control protocols are provided in Appendix F.6 , and representative examples of each subset are shown in Figure 8 .

sections.heading: 3 Diagnosing Squint Text
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, all diagnostic experiments use Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with frozen weights. We report set-matched ANLS for transcription and out-of-fold AUC for probing. The failure is not confined to this checkpoint: four commercial and open-weight MLLMs obtain only 8.3–24.4 ANLS on the original SquintBench images (Table 3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Hidden-Text Representation
sections.text: To test what survives in the vision encoder, we fit logistic-regression probes to frozen, pre-merger patch features at blocks L6/12/18/24/27. Each probe uses mean-pooled features and is evaluated out of fold against shuffled-label controls; fitting it does not update the MLLM. On SquintCtrl-Pair , whose 500 pairs differ only in whether a string was embedded, text presence reaches 0.956–0.981 AUC. Label shuffling returns chance-level performance (0.47–0.52 AUC), while matched generation paths control for synthesis-pipeline artefacts (Appendix A.3 ). Going beyond mere presence, we further test how well each individual glyph can be read out on the closed-vocabulary SquintCtrl-Glyph set. Glyph identity is weaker than presence but remains above chance: Chinese macro-AUC peaks at 0.718 at L18 and averages 0.676 across the five blocks, with Latin at 0.612 and 0.581, respectively. Thus, the encoder detects hidden text, although glyph identity is only weakly represented.

sections.heading: 3.2 Spatial Localization
sections.text: We extract visual features before the patch merger and, using the known SquintCtrl-Glyph mask, compare three poolings of the same features: oracle averages vectors at glyph-bearing locations, global averages all vectors, and random averages a random subset of the same size as the oracle set . Random controls for sample count: its mean estimates the global mean and empirically differs from it by at most 0.004 AUC. Averaged over five blocks, oracle / global / random reach 0.799/0.676/0.675 AUC on Chinese and 0.664/0.581/0.580 on Latin, respectively (Figure 2 a), so oracle improves by about 0.10 AUC over both controls. Glyph identity is therefore substantially more accessible at the correct locations, identifying spatial selection as a major bottleneck ( Wu & Xie, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Passing these features through the patch merger changes separability by at most 0.018 AUC (Appendix A.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Frequency and Token Count
sections.text: That downscaling or low-pass filtering makes such text legible is already established—HC-Bench evaluates after downscaling ( Li et al., 2025 ) and Illusory VQA after low-pass filtering ( Rostamkhani et al., 2025 ) . What is not established is which property of those transforms is responsible, and the answer determines what one should build: ( H1 ) high-frequency texture masks the glyph structure; ( H2 ) too many tokens dilute attention; ( H3 ) it is a contrast problem. We test these explanations on SquintBench images (Figure 2 b). At the original token budget (median 400), Gaussian low-pass filtering raises ANLS from 26.4 to 39.3, showing that suppressing high frequencies helps without shortening the visual sequence. Restricting the visual input to 64 tokens yields 29.2; applying a stronger low-pass transform at the same token budget raises ANLS to 67.0. This matched-budget comparison independently supports H1. However, constructing the 64-token input also alters its frequency content, so H2 cannot be fully disentangled from H1. We additionally test H3 with contrast-only transforms, which yield substantially smaller gains than frequency suppression (Appendix B ), making contrast an unlikely primary explanation. Overall, these results identify high-frequency interference as a major contributor, while visual token count may also contribute, although its effect is not fully disentangled from frequency. Figure 2: Three diagnostics on frozen off-the-shelf weights. (a) Restricting the read-out to glyph-bearing tokens improves glyph-identity prediction, supporting spatial selection as a major bottleneck (per-layer expansion in Appendix A ). (b) At a fixed 64-token budget, suppressing high-frequency content raises squint-text ANLS from 29.2 to 67.0 (per- σ \sigma results in Appendix B ). (c) For the same target glyph 搜, adding a 1 / 8 1/8 -scale view of the same image shifts the base model’s phonetic predictions toward visually matching glyphs, indicating stronger visual grounding.

sections.heading: 3.4 Corrective Viewing
sections.text: We next give the same frozen model the two-view input ⟨ x , v ⟩ \langle x,v\rangle , with no change to its weights or prompt. On SquintBench , adding the 1 / 8 1/8 -scale view raises ANLS from 26.50 to 58.96. Figure 2 c shows the corresponding shift from phonetic alternatives toward candidates that share the target’s visual structure. Because v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) is deterministic and lossy, the gain is consistent with the same frozen weights exploiting coarse visual evidence more effectively under a different viewing condition. The result motivates learning a similar read-out behaviour while retaining original-only input. Design requirements. The diagnosis yields three requirements. (D1) Original-only inference: the solution should receive x x alone, because the needed evidence already survives in its representation. (D2) Localization-bearing supervision: a transcript says what the glyph is but not where its evidence lies, whereas predictions elicited by the downscaled view reflect evidence that has become easier to select. The method should transfer this implicit spatial information; whether it does so is tested in § 6 . (D3) Distributional targets: at each step the teacher assigns probability mass over possible next tokens, not only the ground-truth one; the relative probabilities of alternatives retain which glyphs remain visually plausible — information a one-hot label cannot express. sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: Table 1 suggests supervising the student under a viewing condition in which Squint Text is easier to read. During training, the teacher receives privileged context consisting of the downscaled view and the ground-truth output, while the student receives only the original image. Inference remains original-only. Figure 3 illustrates the training framework.

sections.heading: 4.1 Squint OPSD
sections.text: Let x x be the original image, v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) its downscaled view, q q the task instruction, and h h the ground-truth output provided only to the teacher. The student is p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , q ) p_{\theta}(y\mid x,q) and the teacher is a frozen copy of the initial backbone conditioned on ( x , v , q , h ) (x,v,q,h) . For each step, the teacher’s top- K K tokens define the explicit support; probability mass outside this support is aggregated into a single tail bucket for both teacher and student before computing JSD. The privileged view and the ground-truth hint play different roles. The view changes the visual condition under which the teacher reads the image, whereas the hint supplies privileged label information. Their contributions are separated empirically in Table 4 and Appendix C .

sections.heading: 4.2 Privileged View
sections.text: Since v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) is a deterministic, lossy transform of the original image, it does not introduce new Shannon information conditional on x x . Its value is therefore computational ( Xu et al., 2020 ) : the same visual content can become easier for a fixed model to exploit after high-frequency suppression and scale change. The ground-truth hint h h , by contrast, does provide privileged label information. Accordingly, we do not assume that the complete teacher distribution p T ( ⋅ ∣ x , v , q , h ) p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,v,q,h) is exactly realizable from ( x , q ) (x,q) alone. Our objective is empirical: transfer the components of the teacher’s reading behavior that the student can acquire while retaining original-only inference. Figure 3: Overview of Squint OPSD . The teacher receives the original image, the downscaled view v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) , the task instruction, and the ground-truth output as privileged context. Its token distributions supervise the student along stop-gradient, student-generated trajectories. Gradients flow only through the student logits, and inference uses the original image alone.

sections.heading: Datasets and metrics.
sections.text: We train on 5905 prompts, including 3489 synthetic hidden-text images, 1213 OCR samples, and 1203 VQA samples. Our primary evaluation is set-matched ANLS on all 1076 deployment-derived SquintBench images. We further evaluate transfer on Illusory VQA ( Rostamkhani et al., 2025 ) , AdvOCR ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and HC-Bench ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and general vision-language capability on AI2D ( Kembhavi et al., 2016 ) , DocVQA ( Mathew et al., 2021 ) , and OCRBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . We reserve a 1,045-example held-out validation split from the same source mixture as training.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against the pretrained backbone ( Base ), appending a downscaled view at inference ( Base + 1 / 8 +1/8 view, two-view), single-view SFT, and DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . For trained baselines, we focus on methods that use the original image at inference, matching the deployment constraint of Squint OPSD . We also report four off-the-shelf MLLMs as external references: claude-opus-5, gemini-3.1-pro, gpt-6-astra, and Qwen3-VL-235B-Think.

sections.heading: Model and training.
sections.text: All trained methods use Qwen3.5-9B. Unless stated otherwise, all parameters, including the vision tower, are updated. In the current experiments, the teacher is a frozen copy of the initial backbone and receives the privileged downscaled view and ground-truth hint, while the student receives only the original image. Squint OPSD , DAPO, and SFT are all trained for three epochs. Full optimization and rollout details are in Appendix F.3 ; the held-out mixture is described in Appendix F.2 .

sections.heading: Inference.
sections.text: Squint OPSD receives only the original image at inference. Additional scaled views are provided only to baselines explicitly marked with them.

sections.heading: Target performance.
sections.text: Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench , compared with 26.50 for Base and 58.96 when the corrective view is appended only at inference (Table 2 ). It also exceeds single-view SFT (72.47) and DAPO (73.55). SFT improves the target metric only partway and forgets heavily: its DocVQA falls from 95.93 to 64.73 and OCRBench from 879 to 722. SFT warm starts likewise underperform direct OPSD, suggesting that first fitting a hard one-hot target is less effective than preserving distributional supervision from the outset. We also ran a series of teacher-view ablations that vary only v v in the fixed teacher input ( x , v , q , h ) (x,v,q,h) ; none of the alternative views or their aggregations improves on the default (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: External transfer.
sections.text: The capability transfers to external hidden-text benchmarks (Table 3 ). On original inputs, Squint OPSD reaches 66.7 on AdvOCR and 44.6 on HC-Bench, compared with 3.7 and 1.8 for Base . On Illusory VQA, it reduces WER from 178.10 to 67.00, even outperforming Base given the filtered view (76.80). Increasing model scale alone also does not remove the failure: Qwen3-VL-235B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) reaches only 24.44 on the original SquintBench images, and gpt-6-astra only 8.33.

sections.heading: General-capability trade-off.
sections.text: The hidden-text gain is accompanied by task-dependent degradation on the general benchmarks: AI2D changes from 86.66 to 85.33, DocVQA from 95.93 to 92.98, and OCRBench from 879 to 833. Thus, the adaptation retains substantial general vision-language capability, but introduces a measurable specialization trade-off.

sections.heading: Privileged teacher context.
sections.text: Neither signal alone gets far: hint-only teacher input yields 41.79, view-only yields 54.68, and x x -only yields 27.96. Combining the view and hint reaches 88.61, substantially above either signal alone. Independently, swapping the view for another sample’s downscaled image reduces the paired score from 84.60 to 78.60, and corrupting the hint with a wrong transcription drops it to 64.00. The two privileged signals are therefore complementary, and each must be aligned with the current sample: the view contributes sample-specific visual context rather than merely extra low-resolution tokens, while the hint supplies label information beyond what the view alone provides.

sections.heading: Distributional supervision.
sections.text: Replacing the teacher distribution with its one-hot prediction drops performance from 88.61 to 68.31, below even ground-truth SFT (72.47). The gain therefore comes from information carried by the distribution rather than from better teacher hard labels. Section 6 examines this structure directly.

sections.heading: Where adaptation occurs.
sections.text: Updating only the language side reaches 29.25, whereas updating only the vision tower already reaches 71.12. Joint adaptation further improves to 88.61. Thus, visual adaptation accounts for a large part of the gain, while the strongest read-out requires both sides to adapt. The same dependence appears under supervised fine-tuning (Appendix F.4 ), supporting the representation change analyzed in § 6 .

sections.heading: Teacher and training variants.
sections.text: Entropy-based teacher selection, EMA teacher updates, and SFT warm starts likewise underperform the fixed-teacher recipe (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 6 Analysis
sections.text: We analyze three changes induced by training: glyph representation, spatial selection, and candidate-distribution structure. The probe and candidate-distribution analyses reuse the protocols established in § 3 .

sections.heading: Glyph representations become more discriminative.
sections.text: Re-running the probes from § 3.1 , glyph-identity AUC rises from 0.718 to 0.975 on Chinese and from 0.612 to 0.779 on Latin, while near-ceiling presence detection changes little. Together with the frozen-vision ablation in § 5.3 , this shows that training reorganizes the visual representation to make glyph identity more accessible.

sections.heading: Reading becomes spatially grounded.
sections.text: After training, answer-token attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) is more concentrated on glyph-bearing regions, with similar patterns under free generation and teacher forcing (Figure 4 b). We complement this correlational evidence with a visual-token embedding intervention. Before the visual tokens enter the language model, we replace glyph-bearing embeddings with the mean embedding of non-glyph tokens from the same image, while keeping token count and positions unchanged. At dilation d = 2 d=2 , this reduces Squint OPSD accuracy from 90.5% to 71.5%, whereas replacing an equal number of randomly selected background-token embeddings leaves performance nearly unchanged (90.5% to 91.0%). The result supports a causal dependence of the learned reading behavior on glyph-bearing visual regions. Full intervention details are given in Appendix E.5 .

sections.heading: The distribution acquires visual structure.
sections.text: We compare non-target, high-probability candidates on the same 120 glyph positions valid for all three models. We measure ρ vis \rho_{\mathrm{vis}} as the Spearman correlation between candidate probability and pixel-IoU similarity to the target glyph, and ρ lang \rho_{\mathrm{lang}} as the correlation between candidate probability and its matched text-only probability. Visual organization increases from ρ vis = 0.126 \rho_{\mathrm{vis}}=0.126 for Base to 0.242 for SFT and 0.286 for Squint OPSD . Meanwhile, Squint OPSD retains a text-only-prior correlation close to Base ( ρ lang = 0.544 \rho_{\mathrm{lang}}=0.544 vs. 0.555), whereas SFT drops to 0.334. Thus, Squint OPSD more strongly organizes high-probability alternatives by glyph compatibility while retaining language-side structure. Definitions and candidate-set sensitivity are in Appendix E.1 . sections.heading: Hidden and squint-visible content.
sections.text: HC-Bench studies hidden content with downscaling ( Li et al., 2025 ) , Illusory VQA applies low-pass filtering ( Rostamkhani et al., 2025 ) , and AdvOCR/VACoT learns when to zoom in or out at inference ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; training-free alternatives steer a frozen model’s search toward small visual details ( Wu & Xie, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . These works alter the viewing condition or the search process at inference. To our knowledge, Squint OPSD is the first work on squint-visible hidden text to address this failure through post-training for original-only inference. SquintBench adds deployment-derived failures and SquintCtrl supports controlled diagnosis; the frequency effect is related to hybrid images ( Oliva et al., 2006 ) and image-scaling attacks ( Quiring et al., 2020 ) , a principle recently productized by hidden-content fonts ( Mixfont, 2026 ) , while text-to-image generators render the coarse-structure channel increasingly accessible ( Wu et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: Text-rich reading and privileged supervision.
sections.text: Prior work improves pixel-text understanding through reading-oriented data and architectures ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , benchmarks text-rich comprehension ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and studies the symbolic-to-pixel modality gap ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . Global–local methods provide additional visual views ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and native high-resolution input pipelines enlarge the visual budget available to small text ( Guo et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Related privileged-information and on-policy distillation methods use signals available only during training ( Vapnik & Vashist, 2009 ; Hinton et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . These works largely target fine-grained visual detail retrieval.

sections.heading: Probing visual representations.
sections.text: Linear probes test information in intermediate representations ( Alain & Bengio, 2018 ; Burns et al., 2023 ) , while VLM work localizes object information to visual tokens ( Neo et al., 2025 ) and identifies outlier artifact tokens that distort ViT feature maps ( Darcet et al., 2024 ) . We study coarse text whose identity becomes more accessible at the correct locations and how this changes after adaptation.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce Squint Text, SquintBench , and SquintCtrl to study text embedded in coarse image structure that humans can recover but MLLMs often miss. Our diagnostics implicate spatial selection and high-frequency interference, with visual-token count as a possible additional factor. These findings motivate Squint OPSD , which uses a downscaled view and ground-truth transcription as privileged training context while retaining original-only inference. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench versus 26.50 for the base model and transfers to external hidden-text benchmarks with measurable general-capability trade-offs. After training, glyph identity becomes more discriminative, reading depends on glyph-bearing regions under our visual-token embedding intervention, and high-probability alternatives become more visually structured while retaining language-side structure. The method currently relies on recoverable visual evidence and fixed privileged supervision.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: SquintBench is derived from production content-moderation traffic and contains domains, contact strings and policy-violating promotional material, so it raises privacy and dual-use concerns that the fully synthetic SquintCtrl suite does not. The benchmark is hosted on Hugging Face and will be released openly, but because its images embed real websites, access to the production-derived portion is gated and granted on approved request; we study these patterns solely to improve the robustness of visual moderation.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: We used generative AI tools for code implementation, translation of the Chinese prompt templates, and language editing of the manuscript. All AI-assisted output was reviewed and verified by the authors against the raw evaluation logs and the original sources, and we take responsibility for the final content of this paper.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: Code, the evaluation protocol and the synthetic SquintCtrl suite are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Squint_Text-3456 ; SquintBench is hosted on Hugging Face and will be open-sourced, with the production-derived portion gated behind an approved request. Training, optimisation, prompt and preprocessing details are given in Appendices.

sections.heading: B.1 External-benchmark and preprocessing notes
sections.text: HC-Bench contains 56 hidden-text images. Two readers, evaluated independently with squinting permitted, recovered the hidden text in 35.7% of them on average. We therefore treat HC-Bench as an external transfer benchmark rather than a human-legibility ceiling. For the reduced-view rows in Table 3 , the model preprocessor enforces a minimum input area of 65536 pixels. Both the 1 / 8 1/8 and 40 × 40 40{\times}40 conditions therefore reach the encoder at approximately 256 2 256^{2} pixels and 64 visual tokens. The labels in Table 3 describe the image before this preprocessing step. The 64-token condition of § 3.3 is not the same manipulation as these rows, even though both end at 64 visual tokens. Table 3 replaces the whole image with a reduced view and then lets the preprocessor resize it, whereas § 3.3 pools the original view down to 64 tokens directly; the two therefore differ in spectrum and in score (29.2 versus 38.22 for the base model). Neither number should be read as a replication of the other.

sections.text: All reported default Squint OPSD results use a fixed teacher copied from the initial backbone. The teacher-input ablation in Table 4 separates the privileged view from the ground-truth hint. The view alone reaches 54.68, above the hint-only condition at 41.79; combining both reaches 88.61. A stronger control replaces the teacher’s second view with the 1 / 8 1/8 downscaled view of another sample while keeping the original image, hint, resolution, and visual-token budget unchanged. Under the paired setting, the matched view reaches 84.60 and the mismatched view 78.60; the gap remains through the third epoch. This isolates the benefit of sample-aligned corrective visual context. The target-form ablation provides a separate control. Replacing the teacher’s top- K K distribution with its one-hot prediction reduces performance from 88.61 to 68.31, below ground-truth SFT at 72.47. Thus, the teacher is not simply a better source of hard labels; the distribution itself carries useful supervision.

sections.heading: C.1 Corrective-view and training variants
sections.text: In all experiments, the teacher receives the same original image x x , task instruction q q , and ground-truth hint h h ; we vary only the corrective view v v (Table 10 ). Replacing the default 1 / 8 1/8 view with a fixed 40 × 40 40{\times}40 view retains nearly identical performance (88.09 vs. 88.61), while v = 1 / 4 v=1/4 reaches 78.51. We also tested whether complementary scales could be combined by averaging or selecting among teacher distributions from v ∈ { 1 / 8 , 1 / 4 , 40 × 40 } v\in\{1/8,\,1/4,\,40{\times}40\} ; none improves over the single default teacher, with probability averaging reaching 83.05. Table 10: Teacher-view variants. All Squint OPSD teachers receive ( x , v , q , h ) (x,v,q,h) ; only the corrective view v v or its aggregation is varied. Student inference always uses ( x , q ) (x,q) only. teacher configuration corrective view v v SquintBench default 1 / 8 1/8 88.61 fixed view 40 × 40 40{\times}40 88.09 fixed view 1 / 4 1/4 78.51 probability mean 1 / 8 , 1 / 4 , 40 × 40 1/8,\ 1/4,\ 40{\times}40 83.05 max-entropy selection 1 / 8 , 1 / 4 , 40 × 40 1/8,\ 1/4,\ 40{\times}40 80.51 min-entropy selection 1 / 8 , 1 / 4 , 40 × 40 1/8,\ 1/4,\ 40{\times}40 74.30 Beyond the view itself, updating the teacher by EMA (rate 0.05) reaches 79.12. SFT warm starts reach 82.85 after one epoch and 81.35 after two epochs, both below direct Squint OPSD at 88.61. One plausible explanation is that the supervised stage first concentrates probability on a one-hot target, reducing the uncertainty over visually plausible alternatives that Squint OPSD is designed to transfer. Starting with distributional supervision preserves this structure throughout training. We initially hypothesized that corrective views at different scales might provide complementary teacher signals. We therefore combine the 1 / 8 1/8 , 1 / 4 1/4 , and 40 × 40 40{\times}40 teachers using probability averaging, minimum-entropy selection, and maximum-entropy selection. None exceeds the best single fixed teacher: probability averaging reaches 83.05, while maximum- and minimum-entropy selection reach 80.51 and 74.30, respectively. We think there are two reasons for this. First, the 1 / 8 1/8 and 40 × 40 40{\times}40 teachers are individually strong (88.61, 88.09) while the 1 / 4 1/4 teacher is much weaker (78.51); averaging their distributions therefore lets the weak 1 / 4 1/4 teacher drag down the two strong ones, instead of complementing them. Second, min-entropy selection (74.30) does notably worse than max-entropy selection (80.51): picking the most confident teacher discards exactly the uncertainty that a distributional target is meant to preserve — the spread over visually confusable glyphs — whereas retaining more uncertainty keeps more of the alternative candidates alive for the student to learn from.

sections.heading: Appendix D Recoverability Boundary
sections.text: SquintCtrl-Strength varies only the ControlNet conditioning strength over the same 200 scenes. Both Base and Squint OPSD improve as the glyph signal becomes more visible, but the largest useful margin appears in the partially recoverable regime. At strength 0.5, where strokes are largely destroyed, Base and Squint OPSD are statistically indistinguishable (0.597 vs. 0.615, 95% CI [ − 0.008 , + 0.063 ] [-0.008,+0.063] ; paired bootstrap, 100 resamples). At strength 0.9, Squint OPSD improves from 0.886 to 0.944; at 1.2, both models are near ceiling. This empirically delineates the recoverability boundary of the method: training can reorganize partially recoverable evidence, but does not reconstruct glyph structure that is largely absent from the input. sections.heading: E.1 Candidate-distribution metrics
sections.text: For § 6 , we analyze 200 SquintCtrl-Read images. We retain examples whose ground-truth characters are each represented by a single token, yielding 367 aligned glyph positions before candidate filtering. At each position, we run the model under teacher forcing and take its top- 20 20 next-token candidates. We remove the ground-truth token, retain only tokens that decode to exactly one CJK codepoint, and keep positions with at least five valid candidates. Thus, the analysis concerns non-target high-probability alternatives rather than the full vocabulary tail. For ρ vis \rho_{\mathrm{vis}} , each candidate and target glyph is rendered with Noto Sans CJK SC, centered by its ink bounding box, dilated with a 3 × 3 3{\times}3 max filter, resized to 64 × 64 64{\times}64 with Lanczos resampling ( Lanczos, 1964 ) , and binarized. Visual similarity is pixel IoU. We compute a per-position Spearman correlation between candidate probability and glyph IoU, subtract the mean correlation from 20 random permutations of the similarity scores, and average over valid positions. For ρ lang \rho_{\mathrm{lang}} , we evaluate the same checkpoint without the image, using the identical OCR prompt and teacher-forced ground-truth prefix. We then compute the per-position Spearman correlation between the image-conditioned candidate probabilities and their probabilities under this matched text-only context. Multi-token ground-truth characters are excluded from the analysis.

sections.heading: E.5 Visual-token embedding knockout
sections.text: To test whether reading causally depends on glyph-bearing visual regions, we intervene on the output embeddings of the vision tower before they are passed to the language model. The intervention is applied once during prefill; no language-model attention logits or weights are modified. Let T T denote visual tokens whose receptive fields overlap the known glyph pattern. For the glyph knockout, each embedding in T T is replaced by the mean embedding of the non-glyph tokens from the same image. This preserves sequence length, token positions, and the subsequent attention computation. As a matched control, we sample the same number of tokens uniformly from the non-glyph region using a fixed random seed and apply the identical mean-embedding replacement. We additionally dilate the glyph mask by d ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } d\in\{0,1,2\} iterations of a 3 × 3 3{\times}3 neighborhood operation. These interventions replace on average 169.0 (16.5%), 299.9 (29.3%), and 391.8 (38.3%) of the 1024 visual tokens, respectively. Generation is greedy with a maximum of 64 new tokens, and a prediction is counted as correct when the ground-truth string occurs in the generated transcription after whitespace removal. Table 12 shows that the effect is strongly spatially specific. At d = 2 d=2 , Squint OPSD decreases from 90.5% to 71.5%, while the matched random intervention changes accuracy only from 90.5% to 91.0%. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench , comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl , a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as a major bottleneck. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD : a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories. At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench , versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone, 24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and 68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference. 1 Introduction Multimodal LLMs can miss text embedded in an image’s coarse structure even when a human can recover it by squinting or viewing the image at reduced scale. We call this failure Squint Text ; we study why the visual evidence is difficult for current models to access and show that the corrective viewing condition can be internalized through training, enabling original-only inference. Modern VLMs are strong scene-text readers, yet this capability breaks sharply on Squint Text . As Figure 1 shows, frontier commercial and open-source models ( Singh et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) can report that no text is present even when the hidden string is readily recoverable by a person. The failure also persists with model scale (Table 3 ). Downscaling or low-pass filtering recovers part of the missing text, but leaves a substantial residual. Squint Text therefore exposes a specific recognition deficiency that stronger generic perception and inference-time preprocessing do not reliably remove. This deficiency matters in deployment. Images are widely used to carry illicit promotion and other policy-violating content ( Meta, 2026c ; Meta, 2026b ; X Corp., 2026 ; TikTok, 2026 ) , and the harmful semantics can reside in text drawn into the image rather than in the depicted scene ( Guo et al., 2024a ; Kiela et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) . In production moderation traffic, we observe domains, contact strings, and slogans embedded into coarse image structure so that human viewers can read them while the reviewing model reports no text. Such examples create a direct blind spot at the visual-review stage of an automated moderation pipeline ( Meta, 2026a ) . To study the failure, we introduce SquintBench , containing 1076 production moderation images, and SquintCtrl , a controlled synthetic suite for isolating what the model represents and where the failure arises. Frozen-weight diagnostics show that hidden text leaves a strong coarse signal, while glyph identity is only weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied. Controlled image interventions on SquintBench itself further show that suppressing high-frequency content can substantially improve reading at matched visual-token budgets, implicating high-frequency interference as a major contributor while leaving room for a secondary token-count effect. These findings motivate Squint OPSD : during training, a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distribution supervises a student that sees only the original image. At inference, the student receives the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench , compared with 26.50 for the base model and 58.96 when the corrective view is supplied only at inference. The capability transfers to external hidden-text benchmarks while retaining substantial general vision-language capability with measurable, task-dependent trade-offs. Analysis after training shows that glyph representations become more discriminative, reading depends causally on glyph-bearing regions under our visual-token embedding intervention, and the residual candidate distribution becomes more visually structured. Code and the evaluation suite are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Squint_Text-3456 . Contributions. • A deployment-grounded failure mode and two complementary datasets. We define Squint Text and introduce SquintBench , comprising 1076 production moderation images, for realistic evaluation, together with SquintCtrl for controlled diagnosis of hidden-text representation, localization, and recoverability. • A diagnosis of why current MLLMs miss Squint Text . Hidden text leaves a strong coarse signal but weak glyph identity; the identity signal becomes more accessible at glyph-bearing locations, and high-frequency interference is a major contributor, with token count a possible secondary factor. • A diagnosis-driven training method. Squint OPSD uses a downscaled privileged view together with a ground-truth hint to provide token-level distributional supervision for original-only inference, reaching 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench . Figure 1: Squint Text , and why the deployed defence does not remove it. (a) Pipeline images whose embedded string a human reads—directly or by stepping back—while GPT, Gemini and Claude each answer “No text in this image” , on the original and the scaled view alike. (b) Downscaling before review recovers only part of the hidden text for every off-the-shelf model. 2 Preliminaries and Data 2.1 Problem setting Given an image x x and an instruction to transcribe its text, the model must report every string a human reader would, including text carried in the image’s coarse structure. We use read-out to refer to the mapping from encoded visual representations to the generated transcription. Let v = g ⁡ ( x ) v=g(x) denote a bicubically downscaled view of x x , at 1 / 8 1/8 linear scale unless stated otherwise. We compare a single-image input x x with a two-view input ⟨ x , v ⟩ \langle x,v\rangle to test whether changing the viewing condition makes the same underlying visual evidence easier for a frozen model to use. Section 3 performs this comparison with identical off-the-shelf weights; the training method is introduced separately in Section 4 . On SquintBench we report ANLS ( Biten et al., 2019 ) , with predicted and reference regions matched as a set before scoring so that a correct transcription written in a different order is not penalised. 2.2 Datasets Showing that the phenomenon occurs in deployment requires real model failures; attributing the failure to a particular mechanism requires controlled examples. We therefore use two complementary datasets. SquintBench comprises 1076 squint-text images collected from a production moderation pipeline. All 1076 examples are production-derived. These images are typically profile photos, in which a human reader recognizes the embedded text almost effortlessly. Human annotators transcribe all visible and hidden text. Thus, SquintBench is used as the realistic end-to-end evaluation set. SquintCtrl supplies the controlled counterpart. A glyph string is rendered as a binary conditioning image and embedded into a scene using QR Code Monster v2 ( Monster Labs, 2023 ) , a ControlNet ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) over Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , with scene prompts sampled from JourneyDB ( Sun et al., 2023 ) . For each controlled comparison, non-target generation variables are held fixed; because the conditioning image is known, each sample also has an exact token-level glyph mask without detector or human annotation. The four subsets serve distinct diagnostics. SquintCtrl-Pair contains 500 matched text-present/text-free pairs for testing whether hidden-text presence is encoded. The text-free member is regenerated through the same ControlNet branch using an all-black conditioning image, avoiding a synthesis pipeline shortcut. SquintCtrl-Glyph contains two 500-image closed vocabularies over ten Chinese glyphs ( 加女可度搜月百看网馊) and ten Latin letters for glyph-identity and localization analyses. SquintCtrl-Strength varies 200 scenes across 5 conditioning strengths to study the recoverability boundary. SquintCtrl-Read contains 200 open-vocabulary images for end-to-end read-out and post-training analysis. Detailed generation and control protocols are provided in Appendix F.6 , and representative examples of each subset are shown in Figure 8 . 3 Diagnosing Squint Text Unless stated otherwise, all diagnostic experiments use Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with frozen weights. We report set-matched ANLS for transcription and out-of-fold AUC for probing. The failure is not confined to this checkpoint: four commercial and open-weight MLLMs obtain only 8.3–24.4 ANLS on the original SquintBench images (Table 3 ). 3.1 Hidden-Text Representation To test what survives in the vision encoder, we fit logistic-regression probes to frozen, pre-merger patch features at blocks L6/12/18/24/27. Each probe uses mean-pooled features and is evaluated out of fold against shuffled-label controls; fitting it does not update the MLLM. On SquintCtrl-Pair , whose 500 pairs differ only in whether a string was embedded, text presence reaches 0.956–0.981 AUC. Label shuffling returns chance-level performance (0.47–0.52 AUC), while matched generation paths control for synthesis-pipeline artefacts (Appendix A.3 ). Going beyond mere presence, we further test how well each individual glyph can be read out on the closed-vocabulary SquintCtrl-Glyph set. Glyph identity is weaker than presence but remains above chance: Chinese macro-AUC peaks at 0.718 at L18 and averages 0.676 across the five blocks, with Latin at 0.612 and 0.581, respectively. Thus, the encoder detects hidden text, although glyph identity is only weakly represented. 3.2 Spatial Localization We extract visual features before the patch merger and, using the known SquintCtrl-Glyph mask, compare three poolings of the same features: oracle averages vectors at glyph-bearing locations, global averages all vectors, and random averages a random subset of the same size as the oracle set . Random controls for sample count: its mean estimates the global mean and empirically differs from it by at most 0.004 AUC. Averaged over five blocks, oracle / global / random reach 0.799/0.676/0.675 AUC on Chinese and 0.664/0.581/0.580 on Latin, respectively (Figure 2 a), so oracle improves by about 0.10 AUC over both controls. Glyph identity is therefore substantially more accessible at the correct locations, identifying spatial selection as a major bottleneck ( Wu & Xie, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Passing these features through the patch merger changes separability by at most 0.018 AUC (Appendix A.2 ). 3.3 Frequency and Token Count That downscaling or low-pass filtering makes such text legible is already established—HC-Bench evaluates after downscaling ( Li et al., 2025 ) and Illusory VQA after low-pass filtering ( Rostamkhani et al., 2025 ) . What is not established is which property of those transforms is responsible, and the answer determines what one should build: ( H1 ) high-frequency texture masks the glyph structure; ( H2 ) too many tokens dilute attention; ( H3 ) it is a contrast problem. We test these explanations on SquintBench images (Figure 2 b). At the original token budget (median 400), Gaussian low-pass filtering raises ANLS from 26.4 to 39.3, showing that suppressing high frequencies helps without shortening the visual sequence. Restricting the visual input to 64 tokens yields 29.2; applying a stronger low-pass transform at the same token budget raises ANLS to 67.0. This matched-budget comparison independently supports H1. However, constructing the 64-token input also alters its frequency content, so H2 cannot be fully disentangled from H1. We additionally test H3 with contrast-only transforms, which yield substantially smaller gains than frequency suppression (Appendix B ), making contrast an unlikely primary explanation. Overall, these results identify high-frequency interference as a major contributor, while visual token count may also contribute, although its effect is not fully disentangled from frequency. (D1) Original-only inference: the solution should receive x x alone, because the needed evidence already survives in its representation. (D2) Localization-bearing supervision: a transcript says what the glyph is but not where its evidence lies, whereas predictions elicited by the downscaled view reflect evidence that has become easier to select. The method should transfer this implicit spatial information; whether it does so is tested in § 6 . (D3) Distributional targets: at each step the teacher assigns probability mass over possible next tokens, not only the ground-truth one; the relative probabilities of alternatives retain which glyphs remain visually plausible — information a one-hot label cannot express. The probe and candidate-distribution analyses reuse the protocols established in § 3 . Glyph representations become more discriminative. Re-running the probes from § 3.1 , glyph-identity AUC rises from 0.718 to 0.975 on Chinese and from 0.612 to 0.779 on Latin, while near-ceiling presence detection changes little. Together with the frozen-vision ablation in § 5.3 , this shows that training reorganizes the visual representation to make glyph identity more accessible. Reading becomes spatially grounded. After training, answer-token attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) is more concentrated on glyph-bearing regions, with similar patterns under free generation and teacher forcing (Figure 4 b). We complement this correlational evidence with a visual-token embedding intervention. Before the visual tokens enter the language model, we replace glyph-bearing embeddings with the mean embedding of non-glyph tokens from the same image, while keeping token count and positions unchanged. At dilation d = 2 d=2 , this reduces Squint OPSD accuracy from 90.5% to 71.5%, whereas replacing an equal number of randomly selected background-token embeddings leaves performance nearly unchanged (90.5% to 91.0%). The result supports a causal dependence of the learned reading behavior on glyph-bearing visual regions. Full intervention details are given in Appendix E.5 . The distribution acquires visual structure. We compare non-target, high-probability candidates on the same 120 glyph positions valid for all three models. We measure ρ vis \rho_{\mathrm{vis}} as the Spearman correlation between candidate probability and pixel-IoU similarity to the target glyph, and ρ lang \rho_{\mathrm{lang}} as the correlation between candidate probability and its matched text-only probability. Visual organization increases from ρ vis = 0.126 \rho_{\mathrm{vis}}=0.126 for Base to 0.242 for SFT and 0.286 for Squint OPSD . Meanwhile, Squint OPSD retains a text-only-prior correlation close to Base ( ρ lang = 0.544 \rho_{\mathrm{lang}}=0.544 vs. 0.555), whereas SFT drops to 0.334. Thus, Squint OPSD more strongly organizes high-probability alternatives by glyph compatibility while retaining language-side structure. Definitions and candidate-set sensitivity are in Appendix E.1 . HC-Bench studies hidden content with downscaling ( Li et al., 2025 ) , Illusory VQA applies low-pass filtering ( Rostamkhani et al., 2025 ) , and AdvOCR/VACoT learns when to zoom in or out at inference ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; training-free alternatives steer a frozen model’s search toward small visual details ( Wu & Xie, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . These works alter the viewing condition or the search process at inference. To our knowledge, Squint OPSD is the first work on squint-visible hidden text to address this failure through post-training for original-only inference. SquintBench adds deployment-derived failures and SquintCtrl supports controlled diagnosis; the frequency effect is related to hybrid images ( Oliva et al., 2006 ) and image-scaling attacks ( Quiring et al., 2020 ) , a principle recently productized by hidden-content fonts ( Mixfont, 2026 ) , while text-to-image generators render the coarse-structure channel increasingly accessible ( Wu et al., 2025a ) . Text-rich reading and privileged supervision. Prior work improves pixel-text understanding through reading-oriented data and architectures ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , benchmarks text-rich comprehension ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and studies the symbolic-to-pixel modality gap ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . Global–local methods provide additional visual views ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and native high-resolution input pipelines enlarge the visual budget available to small text ( Guo et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Related privileged-information and on-policy distillation methods use signals available only during training ( Vapnik & Vashist, 2009 ; Hinton et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . These works largely target fine-grained visual detail retrieval. Probing visual representations. Linear probes test information in intermediate representations ( Alain & Bengio, 2018 ; Burns et al., 2023 ) , while VLM work localizes object information to visual tokens ( Neo et al., 2025 ) and identifies outlier artifact tokens that distort ViT feature maps ( Darcet et al., 2024 ) . We study coarse text whose identity becomes more accessible at the correct locations and how this changes after adaptation. 8 Conclusion We introduce Squint Text, SquintBench , and SquintCtrl to study text embedded in coarse image structure that humans can recover but MLLMs often miss. Our diagnostics implicate spatial selection and high-frequency interference, with visual-token count as a possible additional factor. These findings motivate Squint OPSD , which uses a downscaled view and ground-truth transcription as privileged training context while retaining original-only inference. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench versus 26.50 for the base model and transfers to external hidden-text benchmarks with measurable general-capability trade-offs. After training, glyph identity becomes more discriminative, reading depends on glyph-bearing regions under our visual-token embedding intervention, and high-probability alternatives become more visually structured while retaining language-side structure. The method currently relies on recoverable visual evidence and fixed privileged supervision.
